lessons.title: தண்ணீர், அரிசி, சாதம் — water, and rice, the real staple
lessons.gloss: water, and rice — the actual staple food here, not bread — with a widely-cited (if not fully certain) link from arisi to the English word "rice" itself

segments.text: European languages teach "bread" as the staple food. Here, that would be dishonest — bread isn't the everyday staple in Tamil food culture. Rice is, and it comes with one of the most famous (if contested) etymological journeys of any food-word.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: தண்ணீர் — water, literally "cool water"

segments.text: நீர் (nīr, "water"). Everyday Tamil doesn't just say "water" — it says, quite literally, "cool water."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: அரிசி and சாதம் — rice, raw and cooked

segments.text: Tamil, like most of South India, distinguishes the uncooked grain from the cooked dish with two separate words, not one:
அரிசி (arisi) = "rice" (the raw, husked grain) — native Dravidian.

சாதம் (sātam) = "cooked rice" (the meal itself, what's actually eaten) — likely Sanskrit-influenced. Tamil also keeps a native word for the same idea, சோறு (cōṟu) — the two sit side by side as everyday near-synonyms.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Be honest about a famous (contested) word-journey

segments.text: Here's the exciting part, held with appropriate care: many etymologists connect அரிசி (arisi) to the English word "rice" itself — the proposed chain runs Dravidian arisi becomes Greek óryza becomes Latin oryza becomes Old French ris becomes English rice. If true, English speakers have been saying a Dravidian word for centuries without knowing it. But be honest: standard etymological dictionaries mark Greek óryza's origin as genuinely uncertain — a Dravidian source is one widely cited hypothesis among others (an Indo-Aryan vrīhi-related source is also proposed), not a settled, universally agreed fact.

segments.text: What does தண்ணீர் literally mean? ("Cool water" — taṇ "cool" + nīr "water.") What two words does Tamil use for rice, and why two? (அரிசி arisi, raw grain; சாதம் sātam, cooked rice — the raw grain and the cooked meal get separate words.) Is it certain that English "rice" comes from Tamil arisi? (Not certain — it's a widely cited hypothesis via Greek óryza, but that Greek word's origin is genuinely disputed among etymologists.)
